items.title: Microsoft ships its own MAI models to cut OpenAI dependence and undercut on price
items.summary: Microsoft unveiled first-party models — MAI-Code-1-Flash (turns written specs into app/website source) and MAI-Thinking-1 (reasoning, private preview) — aimed squarely at reducing its reliance on OpenAI and lowering costs for developers. The real signal isn't the models themselves but the strategy: Microsoft is turning Foundry (now 11,000+ models, including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Gemini) into a neutral multi-vendor layer where its own cheaper models become the default. If you build on Azure/Foundry, expect MAI defaults and downward price pressure that shifts which model you reach for.

items.title: Qwen 3.7 Plus: frontier-adjacent multimodal agent at ~6x cheaper input than Max
items.summary: Alibaba brought Qwen 3.7 Plus to GA — a multimodal model (text/image/video in) that perceives screens, operates GUIs, and writes code from visual references, at $0.40/$1.60 per 1M tokens. That's roughly 6x cheaper on input than Qwen 3.7 Max while keeping the 1M-token context window and strong coding/agentic scores, making it one of the cheapest options for vision-to-code and long-horizon agent loops. The tradeoff that matters for engineering decisions: it's proprietary, API-only (no open weights), and China-hosted — so weigh data residency and self-hosting before wiring it into a pipeline.

items.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash beats the larger 3.1 Pro on agentic/coding benchmarks at Flash speed
items.summary: Google made Gemini 3.5 Flash generally available at I/O 2026, and the notable part is that a Flash-tier model now outperforms the bigger Gemini 3.1 Pro on hard agentic and coding benchmarks — Terminal-Bench 2.1 (76.2%), MCP Atlas (83.6%) — while running at Flash latencies. That makes a fast model genuinely viable for the inner loop of coding agents and tool-heavy pipelines, not just chat. Pricing is $1.50/$9 per 1M tokens with a 90% cache discount ($0.15/1M cached input); note it's pricier than earlier Flash models, so the real win is intelligence-per-latency rather than rock-bottom cost.
